subject: Quantitative Aptitude
description: CP, SP, profit %, loss %, discount problems

questions.stem: An article is bought for ₹500 and sold for ₹600. The profit percentage is:
questions.explanation: Profit = SP − CP = 600 − 500 = ₹100. Profit % = (Profit / CP) × 100 = (100/500) × 100 = 20 %. A common trap — 16.67 % — is (Profit / SP), which is the incorrect formula. Profit percentage is always on CP, unless the question specifies otherwise.
questions.subject: Quant

questions.stem: A shopkeeper sells a shirt at 10% loss for ₹450. The cost price of the shirt was:
questions.explanation: At 10 % loss, SP = 90 % of CP. So CP = SP / 0.90 = 450 / 0.90 = ₹500. Verify: 10 % loss on ₹500 = ₹50 → SP = 500 − 50 = ₹450. ✓. Trap 495 is what you get if you add 10 % to ₹450 by mistake (which would apply only if ₹450 were CP, not SP).
questions.subject: Quant

questions.stem: A trader marks up an article by 40% and then offers a discount of 20% on the marked price. His actual profit percentage is:
questions.explanation: Let CP = 100. Marked Price = 100 × 1.40 = 140. Discount 20 % on MP → SP = 140 × 0.80 = 112. Profit = 112 − 100 = 12 → Profit % = 12 %. Shortcut — successive-percentage: (+40) and (−20) → 40 − 20 − (40×20)/100 = 12 %. The ordering (mark up then discount) matters in phrasing but the final net is 12 %.
questions.subject: Quant

questions.stem: A fruit seller bought 120 oranges for ₹600. He sold them at 4 oranges for ₹25. His profit percentage is:
questions.explanation: CP per orange = 600 / 120 = ₹5. SP per orange = 25 / 4 = ₹6.25. Profit per orange = 1.25. Profit % = (1.25 / 5) × 100 = 25 %. Alternative — total: 120 oranges sold for 120 × 6.25 = ₹750; profit = 750 − 600 = ₹150; (150/600) × 100 = 25 %.
questions.subject: Quant

questions.stem: A dishonest shopkeeper uses a 900-g weight in place of a 1-kg weight. His profit percentage (assuming he sells at cost price) is approximately:
questions.explanation: The shopkeeper charges the customer the price of 1,000 g of goods but hands over only 900 g. His gain per transaction = 100 g out of 900 g he actually gave out. Profit % = (100/900) × 100 = 11.11 %. Shortcut — Profit % = [(True weight − False weight) / False weight] × 100. Many students wrongly take the base as 1000 (getting 10 %); the correct base is the actual weight handed over.
questions.subject: Quant

questions.stem: If the cost price of 15 articles equals the selling price of 12 articles, the profit percentage is:
questions.explanation: 15 CP = 12 SP → SP/CP = 15/12 = 5/4. So on each article, SP = 1.25 × CP → profit = 25 %. Shortcut — if 'CP of m articles = SP of n articles', profit % = [(m − n)/n] × 100. Here (15 − 12) / 12 × 100 = 25 %.
questions.subject: Quant

questions.stem: By selling an article for ₹480, a dealer loses 4%. For how much should he sell it to make a profit of 6%?
questions.explanation: At 4 % loss, SP = 96 % of CP. So CP = 480 / 0.96 = ₹500. For 6 % profit, new SP = 500 × 1.06 = ₹530. Verify: 6 % of 500 = 30 → SP = 500 + 30 = 530. ✓. Trap ₹520 corresponds to +4 % of 500 (the exact opposite of the loss) — tempting but wrong.

questions.stem: A shopkeeper sells two watches, each at ₹1,200. He gains 20% on the first watch and loses 20% on the second. What is his net result on the combined transaction?

options.option_text: Net loss of 4% on the combined transaction
Net profit of 4% on the combined transaction
Neither profit nor loss — the gains cancel out
Net loss of 2% on the combined transaction

questions.explanation: When two items are sold at the same price with equal profit% and loss%, the net result is always a loss. Net loss% = (common %/10)² = (20/10)² = 4%. CP₁ = 1200/1.2 = ₹1,000; CP₂ = 1200/0.8 = ₹1,500; Total CP = ₹2,500, Total SP = ₹2,400 → Loss = ₹100 = 4% of ₹2,500. Option C is wrong because equal % on different CPs never cancels.

questions.stem: A retailer purchases goods worth ₹800 and additionally spends ₹200 on transportation and storage. He then sells the goods at 15% profit on his total cost. What is the selling price?

options.option_text: ₹920 — 15% profit applied to purchase price ₹800 only
₹1,150 — 15% profit on total cost (₹800 + ₹200)
₹1,000 — selling at total cost without adding any profit
₹1,200 — 50% markup mistakenly applied to ₹800

questions.explanation: Total cost = ₹800 (purchase) + ₹200 (overhead) = ₹1,000. Selling at 15% profit on total cost: SP = 1,000 × 1.15 = ₹1,150. Option A (₹920) is the most common mistake — applying 15% only to the invoice price of ₹800 and ignoring overhead expenses that are part of the cost.

questions.stem: A dealer mixes two grades of rice costing ₹40/kg and ₹60/kg in the ratio 3:2 by weight. At what price per kg must he sell the mixture to earn a 25% profit?

options.option_text: ₹50/kg — 25% profit applied to only the lower grade
₹60/kg — 25% on weighted-average CP of ₹48/kg
₹62.50/kg — 25% on simple mean of ₹50/kg
₹75/kg — 25% profit applied to the higher grade only

questions.explanation: Weighted-average CP = (3×40 + 2×60) / (3+2) = (120+120)/5 = ₹48/kg. SP for 25% profit = 48 × 1.25 = ₹60/kg. Option C (₹62.50) is the classic error — taking the simple arithmetic mean (40+60)/2 = ₹50 instead of the ratio-weighted mean; the 3:2 ratio skews the average toward the cheaper grade.

questions.stem: A manufacturer lists an item at MRP ₹2,000 and offers a trade discount of 30% to the wholesaler. The wholesaler also avails a further 10% cash discount on the post-trade price. What amount does the wholesaler ultimately pay?

options.option_text: ₹1,200 — combined 40% flat discount applied to MRP
₹1,260 — 30% trade discount, then 10% on reduced price
₹1,300 — single equivalent 35% discount applied on MRP
₹1,400 — only the 30% trade discount applied to MRP

questions.explanation: After 30% trade discount: 2,000 × 0.70 = ₹1,400. After 10% cash discount on ₹1,400: 1,400 × 0.90 = ₹1,260. Option A (₹1,200) is the trap — adding 30+10 = 40% and taking 40% off MRP. Successive discounts always yield a higher net price than a single summed discount because the second discount applies to an already-reduced base.

questions.stem: A vendor buys 200 kg of apples at ₹50/kg. During storage, 20 kg get spoiled and are discarded. He sells the remaining apples at ₹70/kg. What is his overall profit percentage on the transaction?

options.option_text: 40% — comparing ₹70 sell price to ₹50 cost, ignoring loss
26% — net profit of ₹2,600 on total investment of ₹10,000
30% — partial adjustment for the 20 kg spoilage loss
20.6% — profit expressed as a fraction of revenue earned

questions.explanation: Total CP = 200 × 50 = ₹10,000. Saleable quantity = 200 − 20 = 180 kg. SP = 180 × 70 = ₹12,600. Profit = ₹2,600. Profit% = (2,600/10,000) × 100 = 26%. Option A (40%) ignores spoilage entirely. Option D (20.6%) is a common error of computing profit as a % of SP (2,600/12,600), not CP.

questions.stem: A merchant marks up goods by 25% above cost price and then offers a discount on the marked price. If his net profit on the transaction is 5%, what is the discount percentage he offered on the marked price?

options.option_text: 16% — discount correctly computed on the marked price
20% — discount amount taken as percentage of cost price
15% — difference between markup rate and profit rate
25% — confusing the discount percentage with the markup

questions.explanation: Let CP = 100. MP = 125 (25% markup). Net profit = 5%, so SP = 105. Discount = MP − SP = 125 − 105 = 20. Discount% = (20/125) × 100 = 16%. Option B (20%) is the trap — 20 is the absolute discount and candidates often express it over CP (100) rather than over MP (125). Option C (15%) is the naive subtraction 25% − 10%... but profit is only 5%, making that route wrong too.

questions.stem: A manufacturer produces an item at ₹500 and sells it to a wholesaler at 20% profit. The wholesaler sells it to a retailer at 15% profit on his cost, and the retailer sells it to the final customer at 10% profit on his cost. How much does the customer pay?

options.option_text: ₹725 — flat 45% combined markup applied to ₹500 cost
₹690 — chain stops at retailer's purchase price only
₹759 — three successive markups: ×1.20 × 1.15 × 1.10
₹817 — each margin computed on selling price, not cost

questions.explanation: Manufacturer → Wholesaler: 500 × 1.20 = ₹600. Wholesaler → Retailer: 600 × 1.15 = ₹690. Retailer → Customer: 690 × 1.10 = ₹759. Option A (₹725) adds all percentages as a flat 45%, ignoring the compounding effect. Option D (₹817) is what you get if each profit% is applied on SP (i.e., SP = Cost/(1 − margin%)), which is a different profit convention not stated in the problem.
